Question #1
```{r}
#a.
scores <- c("Ana" = 78,"Ben" = 92,"Cid" = 85,"Dex" = 92, "Eli" = 67, "Fay" = 88, "Gio" = 74)

#b.
sort(scores)
sort(scores, decreasing = TRUE)

#c.
print(sort(scores))

#d.
subjects <- c("Science", "Math", "English", "Filipino", "PE") 
incomplete <- c(85, NA, 90, 70, NA, 95)
sort(subjects)
sort(incomplete, na.last = TRUE)
```
Question #2
```{r}
# Because names are linked directly to their scores, sorting simply reorganizes the vector records. 
# If the names do not move alongside the values, it will misalign the data and assign incorrect scores to the students.
```

Question #3
```{r}
# Missing values (NA) are risky due to their inherent ambiguity. Simply placing NA at the bottom 
# can be misleading, as the missing score could theoretically be lower than any of the recorded entries.
```

Question #4
```{r}
order(scores) 
sort(scores)
#order() returns the index position, while sort() returns the rearranged values

#a.
#Yes they do. Order() gives the position of a score in a sorted order.
```

Question #5
```{r}
students <- data.frame(
name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli", "Fay", "Gio"),
score = c(78, 92, 85, 92, 67, 88, 74),
section = c("A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A")
)

#a.
students[order(students$score), ]

#b.
students[order(students$score, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```

Question #6
```{r}
sort(scores) 
scores[order(scores)]

# Running order(scores) outputs the indexing sequence required to achieve an ascending sort, rather than 
# the values themselves. Consequently, the raw vector output isn't useful alone; it must be used as an 
# index—such as scores[order(scores)]—to successfully arrange data vectors or data frames.
```

Question #7
```{r}
#sort() returns only sorted values and loses their original positions, so it can't reorder a data #frame without scrambling the rows. Order() returns positions, so students[order(students$score), ] #moves every row as a unit and keeps all columns lined up.
```

Question #8
```{r}
rank(scores)
cbind(scores, rank(scores))

#a.
rank(scores[c(2,4)])

#b.
#When values tie, `rank()` gives each the average of the positions they share, so Ben and Dex  
#both get 1.5 instead of 1 or 2.
```

Question #9
```{r}
#a.
sales <- data.frame( 
  employee = c("Rey", "Sam", "Tin", "Uma", "Val"), 
  units_sold = c(120, 145, 145, 98, 130))

sales$rank <- rank(-sales$units_sold)
sales

#b.
sales[order(sales$units_sold, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```

Question #10
```{r}
# Yes, the order() function can handle both sorting and indexing tasks seamlessly if there are no ties. 
# However, unlike rank(), order() forces a strict sequential line and cannot natively recognize or 
# handle tied values with equal standing.```
